identification: French Art Deco figural mantel clock, about 1930. Long stepped black slate (or black marble) and banded honey/white onyx plinth, 79 cm long, with a quatrefoil (four-lobed) onyx clock case in the centre. Onyx dial with applied gilt Arabic numerals, gilt hands, two winding holes (8-day striking movement). Left: reclining young woman in a cloche cap and long flared-sleeve robe with gilt incised floral pattern, her face and hands in a pale cream material. Right: patinated doe and fawn grazing. The figures look like cold-painted, patinated spelter (zinc alloy), not bronze: the soft casting detail and the brown 'bronzed' finish are typical of the cheaper French spelter garnitures. The cream face and hands are almost certainly ivorine (celluloid or composition), the standard material on these clocks, not ivory. No signature visible in the photos, so 'by George Maxim' is unconfirmed. Georges Maxim (1885-1940) did model spelter ladies for clocks, but many unsigned clocks of this type get attributed to him. A sticker on the base reads 809, which may be a lot number from an earlier Armitage sale, and a card says 'key in office'.

viewing_check: Look on the back of the lady's robe and the base edge for a cast signature (Geo Maxim, Uriano, Limousin etc). Scratch-test is not allowed, but tap the figures: spelter sounds dull and shows grey metal at worn spots, bronze shows yellow-brown. Check the face and hands for celluloid crazing (ivorine) and chips to the onyx. Ask for the key and see if it runs and strikes.
